Content:
The most important distribution in all probability and statistics is the standard normal distribution. This distribution describes the standard normal random variable, usually denoted as [MATH: Z.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- [MATH: Z] is a continuous random variable. Unlike discrete random variables, normally distributed random variables can take any value in the interval [MATH: (-\infty, \infty).]
- Continuous random variables are described using a continuous curve called the probability density function (or pdf). In the case of [MATH: Z,] its pdf is denoted [MATH: f(z).]
- [MATH: f(z)] has the shape of a so-called bell curve. The graph of this function is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/27a35143eb449ca03022cbc518ce838e]

Content:
The graph has the following important properties:

Content:
- The graph is symmetric about the vertical axis.
- The total area under the curve adds up to [MATH: 1.]

Content:
To state that a random variable [MATH: Z] follows a standard normal distribution, we write

Content:
[MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

Content:
In this notation, [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1] refer to the mean [MATH: \mu] and variance [MATH: \sigma^2] of [MATH: Z,] respectively. We'll learn more about this later.

Content:
An important concept regarding the standard normal distribution is that we calculate probabilities using the area under the graph of [MATH: f(z).]

Content:
For example, suppose that the (continuous) random variable [MATH: Z] follows a standard normal distribution:

Content:
[MATH: Z\sim N(0,1)]

Content:
How do we calculate [MATH: P(Z\leq 1)?]

Content:
By definition, this probability is given by the area under the graph of [MATH: f(z)] over the interval [MATH: z\in (-\infty, 1],] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6a5cc5937aa0ba7444b48b7ef5aa02ce]

Content:
It can be shown that this area equals [MATH: 0.8413] to four decimal places. Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: P(Z \leq 1) = 0.8413.]

Content:
Note the following important points:

Content:
- Since [MATH: Z] is continuous, there is no difference between [MATH: P(Z\leq 1)] and [MATH: P(Z < 1).] Therefore,
[MATH: P(Z \lt 1) = 0.8413.]
It doesn't matter whether [MATH: z\in(-\infty, 1]] or [MATH: z\in (-\infty, 1),] the area under the graph is the same.
- The probability that [MATH: Z] equals a specific value is zero! For example,
[MATH: P(Z = 1) = 0.]
This is because the area under the graph of [MATH: f(z)] at the specific value [MATH: z=1] equals zero.

Content:
The last property makes intuitive sense. Since [MATH: Z] can be any value in the interval [MATH: (-\infty,\infty),] the probability of reaching any particular value is vanishingly small.

- [MATH: Z] is a continuous random variable. Unlike discrete random variables, normally distributed random variables can take any value in the interval [MATH: (-\infty, \infty).]
- Continuous random variables are described using a continuous curve called the probability density function (or pdf). In the case of [MATH: Z,] its pdf is denoted [MATH: f(z).]
- [MATH: f(z)] has the shape of a so-called bell curve. The graph of this function is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/27a35143eb449ca03022cbc518ce838e]

Content:
The graph has the following important properties:

Content:
- The graph is symmetric about the vertical axis.
- The total area under the curve adds up to [MATH: 1.]

Content:
To state that a random variable [MATH: Z] follows a standard normal distribution, we write

Content:
[MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

Content:
In this notation, [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1] refer to the mean [MATH: \mu] and variance [MATH: \sigma^2] of [MATH: Z,] respectively. We'll learn more about this later.

Item 2 — Tutorial: Calculating Probabilities Using Areas

Content:
An important concept regarding the standard normal distribution is that we calculate probabilities using the area under the graph of [MATH: f(z).]

Content:
For example, suppose that the (continuous) random variable [MATH: Z] follows a standard normal distribution:

Content:
[MATH: Z\sim N(0,1)]

Content:
How do we calculate [MATH: P(Z\leq 1)?]

Content:
By definition, this probability is given by the area under the graph of [MATH: f(z)] over the interval [MATH: z\in (-\infty, 1],] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6a5cc5937aa0ba7444b48b7ef5aa02ce]

Content:
It can be shown that this area equals [MATH: 0.8413] to four decimal places. Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: P(Z \leq 1) = 0.8413.]

Content:
Note the following important points:

Content:
- Since [MATH: Z] is continuous, there is no difference between [MATH: P(Z\leq 1)] and [MATH: P(Z < 1).] Therefore,
[MATH: P(Z \lt 1) = 0.8413.]
It doesn't matter whether [MATH: z\in(-\infty, 1]] or [MATH: z\in (-\infty, 1),] the area under the graph is the same.
- The probability that [MATH: Z] equals a specific value is zero! For example,
[MATH: P(Z = 1) = 0.]
This is because the area under the graph of [MATH: f(z)] at the specific value [MATH: z=1] equals zero.

Content:
The last property makes intuitive sense. Since [MATH: Z] can be any value in the interval [MATH: (-\infty,\infty),] the probability of reaching any particular value is vanishingly small.

Content:

Content:

Content:
where [MATH: P(Z \leq z)] denotes the probability that [MATH: Z\sim N(0,1)] is less than some fixed value [MATH: z.]
